clinician.trajectory_summary: A 45-year-old man presented with episodic headaches, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, and irritability, along with elevated blood pressure (170/100 mmHg). Laboratory investigations revealed elevated plasma catecholamines and metanephrines. Imaging (MRI/CT) localized a 3 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with local invasion. Following 10 days of phenoxybenzamine, he underwent a laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. Histopathological examination confirmed pheochromocytoma, measuring 3.5 cm, with capsular and vascular invasion. The postoperative period was uneventful, and at six months follow-up, his symptoms had resolved, blood pressure was normal, and repeat imaging showed no tumor recurrence.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with classic symptoms of pheochromocytoma including episodic headaches, palpitations, sweating, anxiety, irritability, and elevated blood pressure.

Biochemical testing showed significantly elevated plasma catecholamines (epinephrine: 550 pg/mL, norepinephrine: 700 pg/mL) and metanephrines (metanephrine: 1800 pg/mL, normetanephrine: 1200 pg/mL), confirming catecholamine excess.
Imaging studies (MRI and CT) localized a 3 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with evidence of local invasion.
Patient underwent laparoscopic left adrenalectomy after medical preparation.
Histopathological examination of the resected mass confirmed the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, measuring 3.5 cm, with capsular and vascular invasion.
Postoperatively, the patient experienced resolution of symptoms and normalization of blood pressure, with no evidence of recurrence at six months.

remaining_uncertainties: Specific details regarding the 'malignancy markers' mentioned in the pathology report and their clinical significance in this case, given the local invasion but negative malignancy markers.
